title: Demons cannot harm those devoted to God
source_text: Ἀλλ᾿ οὐχ, ὡς οἴεται Κέλσος, βλάπτουσιν οἱ ἀληθῶς σατράπαι καὶ ὕπαρχοι καὶ στρατηγοὶ καὶ ἐπίτροποι τοῦ θεοῦ ἄγγελοι τοὺς ὑβρίζοντας· εἰ δέ τινες βλάπτουσι δαίμονες, οὓς ἐφαντάσθη καὶ ὁ Κέλσος. βλάπτουσιν ὡς φαῦλοι καὶ μηδεμίαν σατραπείαν ἢ στρατηγίαν ἢ ἐπιτροπὴν τοῦ θεοῦ ἐγκεχειρισμένοι, καὶ βλάπτουσι τοὺς ὑποκειμένους αὐτοῖς καὶ ὑποτάξαντας ἑαυτοὺς ὡς δεσπόταις ἐκείνοις. τάχα γὰρ καὶ διὰ τοῦτο οἱ καθ᾿ ἕκαστον τόπον εἰς τὰ νενομισμένα βρώματα μὴ δεῖν ἐσθίεσθαι παρανομοῦντες, εἰ μὲν τῶν ὑπὸ τοὺς δαίμονας εἶεν ἐκείνους, βλάπτονται· εἰ δέ τινες τῶν οὐχ ὑπ᾿ ἐκείνους οὐδὲ αὑτοὺς ὑποτάξαντες τῷ τοῦ τόπου δαιμονίῳ, ἐλεύθεροι ἀπὸ τοῦ ὑπ᾿ ἐκείνων παθεῖν, μακρὰν χαίρειν εἰπόντες τοῖς τοιοισδὶ δαιμονίοις, ἄλλοις διὰ τὴν περὶ ἄλλα ἄγνοιαν ἑαυτοὺς ὑποτάξαντες, ὑπ᾿ ἐκείνων πάσχειν δύνανται, ἀλλ᾿ οὐ Χριστιανὸς, ὁ ἀληθῶς Χριστιανὸς καὶ ὑποτάξας ἑαυτὸν μόνῳ τῷ θεῷ καὶ τῷ λόγῳ αὐτοῦ, πάθοι τι ἂν ὑπὸ τῶν δαιμονίων, ἅτε κρείττων δαιμόνων τυγχάνων· καὶ οὐ πάθοι γ᾿ ἂν, ἐπεὶ „παρεμβαλεῖ ἄγγελος κυρίου κύκλῳ τῶν φοβουμένων αὐτὸν καὶ ῥύσεται αὐτοὺς,“ καὶ ὁ ἄγγελος αὐτοῦ „διὰ παντὸς“ βλέπων „τὸ πρόσωπον τοῦ“ „ἐν οὐρανοῖς“ „πατρὸς“ ἀεὶ τὰς εὐχὰς αὐτοῦ ἀναφέρει διὰ τοῦ μόνου ἀρχιερέως τῷ θεῷ τῶν ὅλων, καὶ αὐτὸς συνευχόμενος τῷ ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ ἐπιτροπευομένῳ. μὴ μορμολυττέσθω τοίνυν ἡμᾶς ὁ Κέλσος, ἀπειλῶν τὴν ἀπὸ τῶν δαιμόνων βλάβην ὑφ᾿ ἡμῶν ἀμελουμένων· οὐδὲν γὰρ ἡμῖν δαίμονες ἀμελούμενοι ποιεῖν ἂν δύναιντο, ἀνακειμένοις τῷ μόνῳ βοηθεῖν πᾶσι τοῖς ἀξίοις δυναμένῳ, ἐφιστάντι δ᾿ οὐδὲν ἧττον καὶ τοὺς ἰδίους ἀγγέλους τοῖς εἰς αὐτὸν εὐσεβοῦσιν, ἵνα μηδὲν οἱ ἐναντίοι ἄγγελοι μηδ᾿ ὁ τούτων „ἄρχων“ λεγόμενος „τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου“ ἐνεργεῖν κατὰ τῶν ἀνακειμένων τῷ θεῷ δυνηθῇ.
pass_a_gloss: But not, as Celsus thinks (οἴομαι), do the truly (ἀληθῶς) satraps and governors and generals and procurators of God, angels (ἄγγελοι), harm (βλάπτω) those insulting (ὑβρίζω) them; but if some demons (δαίμονες) harm, whom Celsus also imagined (φαντάζομαι), they harm as base (φαῦλος) and entrusted (ἐγχειρίζω) with no satrapy (σατραπεία) or generalship (στρατηγία) or stewardship (ἐπιτροπή) of God, and they harm those subject (ὑπόκειμαι) to them and having subjected (ὑποτάσσω) themselves to them as masters (δεσπότης). For perhaps also for this reason those in each place transgressing (παρανομέω) regarding the foods (βρῶμα) customarily held (νομίζω) not to be eaten, if they are of those under those demons, are harmed; but if some are of those not under them nor having subjected themselves to the demon (δαιμόνιον) of the place, [they are] free (ἐλεύθερος) from suffering (πάσχω) by them; having said a long farewell (μακρὰν χαίρειν εἰπόντες) to such demons, having subjected themselves to others through ignorance (ἄγνοια) about other things, they can suffer by those; but a Christian, the truly Christian, and having subjected himself to God alone and to his Word (λόγος), would not suffer anything by demons, as being stronger (κρείττων) than demons; and he would not suffer, since 'an angel of the Lord will encamp (παρεμβάλλω) around those fearing him and will rescue (ῥύομαι) them,' and his angel continually beholding the face of the Father in the heavens always carries up (ἀναφέρω) his prayers through the only high priest (ἀρχιερεύς) to the God of the universe (ὁ θεὸς τῶν ὅλων), himself also praying together with (συνεύχομαι) the one under his guardianship (ἐπιτροπεύω). Let Celsus then not frighten us with bogeys (μορμολύττομαι), threatening the harm (βλάβη) from demons neglected (ἀμελέω) by us; for demons neglected could do nothing to us, devoted (ἀνάκειμαι) to the one alone able to help (βοηθέω) all the worthy (ἄξιος), and no less setting over (ἐφίστημι) his own angels for those pious (εὐσεβέω) toward him, so that neither the opposing (ἐναντίος) angels nor the one called their 'ruler (ἄρχων) of this age (αἰών)' may be able to act (ἐνεργέω) against those devoted to God.
pass_b_english: But the true satraps, governors, generals and procurators of God, the angels, do not harm those who insult them, as Celsus thinks. And if some demons, of the kind Celsus too has pictured, do harm, they harm as wicked beings who have been entrusted by God with no satrapy, command or stewardship; and they harm those who are subject to them and have submitted to them as masters.

Perhaps it is for this reason too that people in each place who break the law about foods that custom says must not be eaten are harmed, if they are among those under those demons. But if some are not under them and have not submitted themselves to the demon of the place, they are free from suffering at their hands, having bidden a long farewell to such demons; yet if, through ignorance about other things, they have submitted themselves to other demons, they can suffer at the hands of those.

But a Christian, a true Christian, who has submitted himself to God alone and to his Word, would suffer nothing from demons, since he is stronger than demons. And he would certainly suffer nothing, since “the angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him, and will deliver them” (Psalm 34:7), and his angel, who “always” beholds “the face of the Father in heaven” (Matthew 18:10), ever carries up his prayers through the only High Priest to the God of the universe, and himself prays together with the one entrusted to his care.

So let Celsus not frighten us with bogeys, threatening us with harm from the demons if we neglect them. For demons, if neglected, could do nothing to us who are devoted to the One who alone is able to help all who are worthy, and who no less sets his own angels over those who are devout toward him, so that neither the opposing angels nor the one who is called their “ruler of this age” (compare 1 Corinthians 2:6; John 12:31) can do anything against those who are devoted to God.

choices.choice: Psalm 34:7 = LXX Psalm 33:8. The middle sentence about food taboos is loose in the Greek: a string of participles without connectives (ἐλεύθεροι ... εἰπόντες ... ὑποτάξαντες ... δύνανται). I read it as: those not under the local demon escape it, but having renounced these demons they may have submitted to others through ignorance and so suffer from them. ‘The only High Priest’ is a title of Christ from Hebrews (compare Hebrews 4:14; 8:1), left uncited inline because it is a title, not a quotation. ‘Ruler of this age’: the singular phrase is not found verbatim; nearest are 1 Corinthians 2:6, 8 (‘rulers of this age’, plural) and John 12:31 (‘ruler of this world’); cited as 1 Corinthians 2:6 for the wording τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου. μορμολυττέσθω rendered ‘try to frighten us like children with bogeys’. Reviewer: inline citation changed to ‘compare 1 Corinthians 2:6; John 12:31’, since neither verse has the singular phrase verbatim.

food-taboo sentence recast: 'having bidden a long farewell' kept with the free group; ὑποτάξαντες made a plain condition ('yet if ... they have submitted ... they can suffer'), removing the supplied 'may have'
'not try to frighten us like children with bogeys' -> 'not frighten us with bogeys' (no added conative or 'like children')
ἐφιστάντι restored as a relative clause on God ('and who no less sets his own angels')
'ruler of this age' citation -> 'compare 1 Corinthians 2:6; John 12:31' (allusion, not verbatim)

anf_compare.notes: Crombie (ANF 1872) and Chadwick (1953) were not used or consulted; the English is from the Greek.
